implementation_notes: System.Threading.Channels turns the pattern into configuration: Channel.CreateBounded<T>(new BoundedChannelOptions(capacity) { FullMode = ... }) with BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait (block the writer until room), DropWrite (refuse the new item), DropOldest or DropNewest, and writer.TryWrite returning false when the item was refused. Because the API is async, the Wait policy suspends the writer instead of blocking a thread, and ReadAllAsync gives the consumer an awaitable loop, so no extra queue or signalling code is needed. Reach for BlockingCollection<T> only in synchronous code or on older frameworks; the channel is the modern default.
pitfalls: DropOldest/DropNewest evict silently: TryWrite still returns true even though an item was lost, so the decision is only observable through your own counters or a depth check.
SingleReader/SingleWriter are performance promises, not hints: setting them while several tasks really do read or write breaks the ordering guarantees.
Awaiting channel operations under a single-threaded SynchronizationContext (UI) or blocking on them with .Result/Wait can deadlock the very thread that would drain the channel.

variants.name: BlockingCollection<T> with boundedCapacity (synchronous)
variants.implementation_notes: For thread-based code BlockingCollection is still the direct expression of the pattern: the constructor takes boundedCapacity, Add blocks while the collection is full, TryAdd returns false instead of waiting, and TryAdd(item, timeout) bounds the wait - the same three outcomes as a queue's put/offer/add, plus a consuming enumerable for the workers. It is disposable and shares one bound across every producer and consumer, which is why it remains the simpler choice in legacy or plain-threaded code. Prefer the bounded channel in async code, where waiting must not pin a thread.
pitfalls: TryAdd returns false both when the collection is full and when it is completed: distinguish the two via IsAddingCompleted, or shutdown looks like back-pressure.
BlockingCollection is IDisposable; not disposing it leaks the internal synchronisation primitive, and completing without draining discards whatever was queued.
Sharing one bounded collection between unrelated workloads lets a single slow producer/consumer pair stall all of them.
